Luke 1.audience: Luke addresses "most excellent Theophilus" and says he has carefully gathered accounts from eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). The same author wrote Acts (Acts 1:1).

culture.title: Courses of priests
culture.text: Priests were divided into twenty-four courses, each serving in the temple for a week at a time (1 Chronicles 24:10 names the course of Abijah). Offering incense was chosen by lot and might happen once in a lifetime.

culture.title: Barrenness
culture.text: Childlessness was seen as a reproach. Elisabeth's story parallels Sarah (Genesis 18) and Hannah (1 Samuel 1).

culture.title: Naming on the eighth day
culture.text: Boys were circumcised on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12) and named then, often after a relative.

Luke 2.audience: Luke dates Jesus' birth by the Roman emperor Caesar Augustus and the governor Cyrenius (Luke 2:1–2), placing the story in world history.

culture.title: The census
culture.text: Roman censuses were used for taxation. Papyri from Egypt show people returning to their home districts to register.

culture.title: The manger
culture.text: A manger was a feeding trough. Village houses often had a lower area where animals were kept at night; the ‘inn’ may mean a guest room.

culture.title: Purification and redemption
culture.text: After childbirth a mother offered a lamb, or two birds if poor (Leviticus 12:8). Mary and Joseph bring "a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons."

Luke 3.audience: Luke dates John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, naming Pilate, Herod, Philip, Lysanias, Annas, and Caiaphas (Luke 3:1–2), about AD 28–29.

culture.title: Publicans and soldiers
culture.text: Tax collectors could add their own charges, and soldiers were known to extort money. John tells them to collect no more than is appointed and to be content with their wages.

culture.title: The genealogy
culture.text: Luke traces Jesus' line back through David and Abraham to "Adam, which was the son of God," while Matthew starts with Abraham.

Luke 4.audience: After the temptation, Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and is driven out of town.

culture.title: Reading in the synagogue
culture.text: A reader stood to read the scroll, handed it back to the attendant, and sat down to teach.

culture.title: The brow of the hill
culture.text: Nazareth was built on a hillside with steep slopes nearby.

culture.title: Widows and lepers
culture.text: Jesus cites the widow of Sarepta (1 Kings 17) and Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5), both foreigners.

Luke 5.audience: Jesus calls Simon, James, and John after a great catch of fish, and heals a leper and a paralyzed man.

culture.title: Lake of Gennesaret
culture.text: Luke calls the Sea of Galilee the lake of Gennesaret, after the plain on its northwest shore.

culture.title: Washing nets
culture.text: Fishermen worked at night with nets and cleaned and mended them in the morning.

culture.title: Through the tiling
culture.text: Luke describes the roof as tiling, a style familiar to readers across the Greek world.

Luke 6.audience: After praying all night, Jesus chooses twelve apostles and gives a sermon on a level place (Luke 6:12–17).

culture.title: Rubbing grain
culture.text: Picking grain by hand from a neighbor's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25). Pharisees counted rubbing it out as work on the sabbath.

culture.title: Good measure
culture.text: Grain sellers filled a measure, pressed it down, and shook it to settle the grain. The buyer carried it in the fold of a robe, called the "bosom."

Luke 7.audience: Jesus heals a centurion's servant, raises a widow's son at Nain, and is anointed by a sinful woman at a Pharisee's house.

culture.title: A centurion who built a synagogue
culture.text: Some Gentiles admired Judaism and supported synagogues. The remains of a fourth-century synagogue at Capernaum stand on top of earlier foundations.

culture.title: Funeral processions
culture.text: Burial happened the same day. The body was carried on an open bier outside the town, followed by mourners.

culture.title: Reclining at table
culture.text: Guests reclined on their left side with feet stretched away from the table, so the woman could stand behind at Jesus' feet.

Luke 8.audience: Luke names women who traveled with Jesus and supported him from their own means, including Joanna, wife of Herod's steward (Luke 8:1–3).

culture.title: Sowing
culture.text: Seed was scattered by hand, sometimes before plowing, so some fell on paths and rocky ground.

culture.title: The Gadarenes
culture.text: The region across the lake from Galilee was largely Gentile, which explains the herd of swine.

Luke 9.audience: Jesus sends out the twelve, feeds five thousand, is transfigured, and "stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51).

culture.title: Shaking off the dust
culture.text: Shaking dust from the feet was a public sign of breaking off contact.

culture.title: Samaritans and pilgrims
culture.text: Samaritans worshiped at Mount Gerizim rather than Jerusalem and sometimes refused hospitality to Jews traveling to Jerusalem's feasts.

culture.title: Bury my father
culture.text: Burying a parent was a central family duty in Jewish life.

Luke 10.audience: Jesus sends out seventy, tells the parable of the good Samaritan, and visits Martha and Mary.

culture.title: The Jericho road
culture.text: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops about 3,300 feet in roughly 17 miles through desert hills, a place known for robbers.

culture.title: Oil and wine
culture.text: Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them; both were common remedies.

culture.title: Two pence
culture.text: A penny (denarius) was a day's wage, so two would pay for several days at an inn.

Luke 11.audience: Jesus teaches the disciples to pray and pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers at a meal.

culture.title: A friend at midnight
culture.text: Families slept together on a raised floor in one room, and the door was barred at night. Hospitality required feeding an arriving guest.

culture.title: Tithing herbs
culture.text: Pharisees tithed even garden herbs like mint and rue.

culture.title: Whitewashed graves
culture.text: Touching a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16). Unmarked graves could be walked over without knowing.

Luke 12.audience: Jesus warns a crowd of thousands about hypocrisy, greed, and worry, and tells them to be ready for the master's return.

culture.title: Sparrows
culture.text: Sparrows were the cheapest birds in the market: five for two farthings.

culture.title: Building bigger barns
culture.text: Grain was stored in barns and storehouses.

culture.title: Loins girded
culture.text: Long robes were tucked into a belt for work or travel.

Luke 13.audience: Jesus speaks about recent disasters, heals a woman bent for eighteen years, and laments over Jerusalem.

culture.title: Pilate and the Galileans
culture.text: Luke is the only source for this killing of Galileans at their sacrifices; Josephus records other violent acts by Pilate.

culture.title: The tower in Siloam
culture.text: Siloam was in the southern part of Jerusalem, near the pool of Siloam.

culture.title: That fox
culture.text: Jesus calls Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, "that fox."

Luke 14.audience: At a sabbath meal at a Pharisee leader's house, Jesus speaks about seating, guests, and the great supper.

culture.title: Seats of honor
culture.text: Places at a feast were ranked; the host could move a guest up or down in front of everyone.

culture.title: Invitations
culture.text: A first invitation was followed by a servant's call when the meal was ready. Refusing at that point was an insult.

culture.title: Counting the cost
culture.text: Towers in vineyards served as watchtowers and shelters.

Luke 15.audience: Tax collectors and sinners gather to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes complain, so he tells three parables of lost things (Luke 15:1–3).

culture.title: Ten pieces of silver
culture.text: Village houses had small windows and earthen floors, so finding a coin required a lamp and a broom.

culture.title: Asking for the inheritance
culture.text: Under the law the elder son received a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17), so the younger would receive a third.

culture.title: Feeding swine
culture.text: Pigs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:7). The husks were probably carob pods used as animal feed.

Luke 16.audience: Jesus tells the parable of the unjust steward and of the rich man and Lazarus. The Pharisees, "who were covetous," scoff (Luke 16:14).

culture.title: Stewards and debts
culture.text: A steward managed an estate's business. A hundred measures of oil and of wheat were large amounts.

culture.title: Purple and fine linen
culture.text: Purple dye, made from murex sea snails, was very costly and worn by the wealthy.

culture.title: Abraham's bosom
culture.text: Reclining next to the host at a banquet put a guest at his bosom (John 13:23).

Luke 17.audience: Between Samaria and Galilee, Jesus heals ten lepers; the only one who returns to thank him is a Samaritan (Luke 17:11–18).

culture.title: A millstone
culture.text: A large millstone was turned by a donkey; a smaller one was turned by hand by women (Luke 17:35).

culture.title: Lepers stood afar off
culture.text: People with skin disease had to live apart and keep their distance (Leviticus 13:45–46).

culture.title: Show yourselves unto the priests
culture.text: A priest had to confirm healing before a leper could return to the community (Leviticus 14).

Luke 18.audience: Jesus tells parables on prayer, blesses children, and speaks with a rich ruler as he nears Jericho.

culture.title: Widows and judges
culture.text: Widows had few legal protectors; the law commanded justice for them (Exodus 22:22).

culture.title: Fasting twice a week
culture.text: Some devout Jews fasted on Mondays and Thursdays, more than the law required.

culture.title: Smote upon his breast
culture.text: Beating the breast was a gesture of grief or remorse (Luke 23:48).

Luke 19.audience: Jesus stays with Zacchaeus in Jericho, tells the parable of the pounds, enters Jerusalem, and weeps over the city.

culture.title: Chief among the publicans
culture.text: Jericho was a wealthy city on a trade route, with balsam groves and palm plantations. Zacchaeus oversaw other tax collectors there.

culture.title: Fourfold restitution
culture.text: The law required fourfold repayment for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1).

culture.title: A nobleman receiving a kingdom
culture.text: Herod's son Archelaus went to Rome to receive his kingdom, and a Jewish delegation followed to oppose him (Josephus).

Luke 20.audience: In the temple, the chief priests, scribes, and Sadducees question Jesus' authority and test him on taxes and resurrection.

culture.title: Absentee landlords
culture.text: Wealthy owners leased vineyards to tenants and sent servants to collect a share of the harvest.

culture.title: Sadducees
culture.text: The Sadducees, a priestly party, denied the resurrection.

culture.title: Levirate marriage
culture.text: If a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow (Deuteronomy 25:5–6).

Luke 21.audience: Jesus praises a poor widow's gift and foretells Jerusalem "compassed with armies" (Luke 21:20). The Romans destroyed the city in AD 70.

culture.title: The treasury
culture.text: Thirteen trumpet-shaped chests in the temple court received offerings.

culture.title: Goodly stones and gifts
culture.text: The temple was decorated with gifts, including a golden vine (Josephus).

Luke 22.audience: Luke tells of Judas' agreement, the Last Supper, the prayer on the Mount of Olives, the arrest, and Peter's denial.

culture.title: Unleavened bread and Passover
culture.text: The Passover lamb was killed on the fourteenth of Nisan, followed by the seven-day feast of unleavened bread (Leviticus 23:5–6).

culture.title: Benefactors
culture.text: Rulers and rich patrons were honored with the title ‘Benefactor’ in public inscriptions.

culture.title: Sweat as drops of blood
culture.text: This verse and verse 43 are missing from some early manuscripts.

Luke 23.audience: Only Luke records that Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, who was in Jerusalem for the feast (Luke 23:6–12).

culture.title: Herod and Pilate
culture.text: Galilee was Herod's territory, so Pilate sent Jesus, a Galilean, to him.

culture.title: Daughters of Jerusalem
culture.text: Women wept and mourned as the condemned were led out.

culture.title: Joseph of Arimathaea
culture.text: A member of the council asked for Jesus' body and buried it in a new rock-cut tomb. Bodies of executed criminals were usually not given honorable burial.

Luke 24.audience: Luke records the empty tomb, two disciples on the road to Emmaus, Jesus appearing in Jerusalem, and his ascension near Bethany.

culture.title: Emmaus
culture.text: Emmaus was about sixty furlongs (roughly seven miles) from Jerusalem.

culture.title: Breaking bread
culture.text: At meals the host took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to the guests.

culture.title: Moses, prophets, and psalms
culture.text: Jesus names the parts of the Hebrew Scriptures: the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms.
